clue.text: Self-identifying followers of 17 somehow seem actively sent kind — wow!

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the following words are to be put together in some other order

explanation.surface: An odd exclamation of surprise at people being sent off in a hurry and kindly.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera Patience, the chorus of lovelorn girls following the poet Bunthorne (17) introduce themselves with this line, so 'Self-identifying' is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: In the opera the chorus of admirers of Bunthorne sing this line to name themselves, so it identifies his followers.

clue.text: He brought order anagrammatically — without hesitation, an outstanding person

indicators.note: anagrammatically openly tells the solver to rearrange the words He brought order
without says some letters are dropped from the words before rearranging

parts.note: er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: A dry remark about rearranging letters, ending in praise for someone exceptional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes ER (hesitation) from HE BROUGHT ORDER, and 'anagrammatically' rearranges the twelve letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: A thoroughbred is figuratively a person of excellent quality or breeding, a first-rate individual.

clue.text: Order to change leader of Conservatives brought in

indicators.note: brought in says one piece is placed inside another

parts.note: to edit a text is to change it

indicators.note: leader of picks the first letter of Conservatives

explanation.surface: An instruction to replace the head of the Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' looks like a command to the reader; it is the definition, a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An edict is an official decree or command issued by an authority.

clue.text: Tree in Bath, possibly not a Mediterranean tree

indicators.note: possibly suggests the words Tree in Bath could be arranged another way
not says the following letter is to be left out of the pool

explanation.surface: Musing about a tree growing in the English city of Bath, perhaps not a southern European one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' removes the A from TREE IN BATH, and 'possibly' rearranges the nine letters left. Bath is a city in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The terebinth is a small turpentine-yielding tree native to the Mediterranean region.

clue.text: Passionate desire — something sailor had for a number of years?

parts.note: lust is strong passionate desire
rum was the traditional daily ration of sailors in the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Linking a sailor's strong urges with his daily tot.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the definition is vague: the number is five.
explanation.definitionFit: A lustrum is a period of five years, originally the interval between Roman purification ceremonies.

clue.text: Gloria's man I saw in Rome embracing another woman

indicators.note: embracing says one piece wraps round another

parts.note: vidi is Latin for I saw, as in Caesar's veni, vidi, vici
Val is a woman's name, short for Valerie

explanation.surface: A woman called Gloria's partner seen in Rome hugging a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Gloria looks like a woman's name; it is the famous sacred choral work, so her man is its composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Vivaldi wrote a celebrated Gloria, so the composer is the man behind that work.

clue.text: Pair were at table spread around — each one a fussy eater

indicators.note: spread around says the outer piece is stretched round another

parts.note: people who sat were seated at a table

explanation.surface: A couple dining at a laden table, each of them picky about food.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Jack Sprat could eat no fat and his wife could eat no lean, so each of the pair was choosy.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack and his wife in the rhyme share the surname, and each refused part of the meat.

clue.text: They come to new home: on island without street?

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first piece sits above the next

parts.note: the punctuation mark printed in the clue is itself a colon

indicators.note: without here means outside, so one piece goes round another

explanation.surface: Settlers arrive on an island that has no roads.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon printed between 'home' and 'on' is itself part of the wordplay, a rare trick; in a down clue 'on' stacks it above the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonists are settlers who leave their country to make a new home in a colony.

clue.text: Twig I found in plant right at the end

indicators.note: found in says a piece is placed inside another
at the end says the named letter shifts to the final position

parts.note: a rose is a flowering plant

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a sprig in a plant at the right-hand edge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the end' moves R (right) from the front of ROSE to make OSER, and 'found in' puts I inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An osier is a willow shoot, the pliant twig used in basket-making.

clue.text: Very badly cut off, having got to isle

parts.note: to sever is to cut off
Ely in Cambridgeshire is the Isle of Ely

explanation.surface: Someone badly cut off after reaching an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Ely is a historic area of Cambridgeshire, in eastern England, once surrounded by fen.
explanation.definitionFit: Severely means seriously or grievously, as in badly injured, so it means very badly.

clue.text: There's my park being redeveloped for big stores

indicators.note: being redeveloped says the letters are rebuilt into a new layout

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A complaint that a local park is being built over for superstores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being redeveloped' rearranges THERES MY PARK.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypermarkets are very large out-of-town stores, bigger than supermarkets.

clue.text: No 10 associated with country's revolution

explanation.surface: Something tied to Downing Street and a national uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 10' suggests Downing Street; it means the tenth month. The second definition is Russia's 1917 revolution, named after the month by the old calendar.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the tenth month, and the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 is called the October Revolution.

clue.text: Hidden potential of learner with a tendency to avoid study

parts.note: L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

indicators.note: to avoid says some letters are kept out of the word tendency

parts.note: a den is a private room for study

explanation.surface: A trainee tends to dodge schoolwork despite talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to avoid' takes DEN (study) out of TENDENCY to leave TENCY.
explanation.definitionFit: Latency is the state of being present but not yet developed or shown, so a hidden potential.

clue.text: Physician dealt with wind and indigestion finally

parts.note: a gale is a strong wind

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of indigestion

explanation.surface: A doctor treating a patient for flatulence and an upset stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' and 'indigestion' suggest a medical complaint; wind is the weather sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Galen was the celebrated Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose medical writings dominated for centuries.

clue.text: Learner's elation unrestrained — first in English with fine marks

parts.note: L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

indicators.note: unrestrained lets the letters of elation run loose into a new order
first in picks the opening letter of English

explanation.surface: A student's wild joy at coming top in English with good grades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unrestrained' rearranges ELATION into INEOLAT.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany and zoology lineolate means marked with fine lines, a fitting phrase for its meaning.

clue.text: See 1
I shouted audibly, being stared at

indicators.note: audibly says the words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: taken as I bawled, since to bawl is to shout

explanation.surface: Someone yelling while people gawp at them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audibly' turns 'I bawled' into the sound of the answer: I as EYE and BAWLED as BALLED.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare at them hard, so being eyeballed is being stared at.

clue.text: Companion lost from group — another ace gone, sadly

indicators.note: lost from says some letters are removed from the word before

parts.note: a bunch is a group
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

indicators.note: sadly signals that the remaining letters are jumbled
gone says the named letter has left the word another

parts.note: a is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: A mourner notes a member has left the group and another star has died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost from' takes CH from BUNCH to leave BUN; 'gone' removes A from ANOTHER and 'sadly' rearranges NOTHER into THORNE. Bunthorne is the poet in Patience, honoured by the preamble.
explanation.definitionFit: The preamble names this character as the person remembered, the aesthetic poet of Gilbert and Sullivan's opera.

clue.text: Country with soldiers in revolution — madness!

indicators.note: in revolution says the piece next to it is turned back to front

parts.note: OR stands for other ranks, ordinary soldiers
mania is madness

explanation.surface: A nation in uprising with its troops gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for other ranks is a crossword convention for ordinary soldiers; 'revolution' also nods to Romania's 1989 uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: Romania is a country in south-eastern Europe, which saw a violent revolution in 1989.

clue.text: A character starting trade needs to organise a bit of capital

indicators.note: to organise says the letters are put in a new arrangement
character starting picks the opening letter of trade

explanation.surface: Advice that a business needs some funding to get set up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to organise' rearranges A, T and NEEDS. 'capital' looks like money; it is London, and this is a district of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The East End is a district of London, the capital, so it is a part of that city.

clue.text: Oaks may be seen here in Surrey

definitions.text: Oaks may be seen here in Surrey

parts.words: Oaks may be seen here in Surrey
parts.note: trees seem meant, but the Oaks is a classic horse race for fillies held at a Surrey racecourse

explanation.walkthrough: The Oaks is one of England's five Classic flat races, run each summer on the Downs near the town that names the course.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom is a Surrey town whose racecourse stages the Oaks and the Derby.

clue.text: It may be evident in some git showing off

definitions.text: It may be evident in some git showing off

indicators.note: off means wrong or out of place, so the letters of some git are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Self-importance shows in an unpleasant person who shows off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges SOME GIT; the whole clue also defines the answer. Git is British slang for an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: Egotism, excessive self-regard, is what a boastful unpleasant person displays.

clue.text: Not the cleverest? Find him out, regularly lacking

indicators.note: regularly lacking drops every other letter, keeping the even ones of Find him out

explanation.surface: A call to track down a dim person.
explanation.walkthrough: From FINDHIMOUT drop the first, third, fifth letters and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot is a stupid person, someone who is far from the cleverest, as the question mark hints.

clue.text: Man's man? Not one for malicious words

indicators.note: Not says the following letter is to be removed

parts.note: a native of the Isle of Man is a Manx islander
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A question about a manly type, then a remark against abuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man's man' looks like a macho type; it means someone from the Isle of Man, an island between Britain and Ireland. 'Not one' removes I.
explanation.definitionFit: Slander is false, damaging spoken statements, a form of malicious words.

clue.text: One with a gift, accomplished — tribute's conclusion

parts.note: done means accomplished or completed

indicators.note: conclusion picks the final letter of tribute

explanation.surface: Someone gifted has finished paying tribute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a gift' suggests talent; it means receiving a present.
explanation.definitionFit: A donee is the recipient of a gift, the person to whom something is donated.

clue.text: Card game was loved by 17

explanation.surface: A solitaire pastime that a certain character adored.
explanation.walkthrough: In the opera named after her, the milkmaid Patience is loved by the poet Bunthorne (17).
explanation.definitionFit: Patience is the one-player card game, and the milkmaid heroine of Gilbert and Sullivan's opera.

clue.text: Weapon of knight — item to be sold off

indicators.note: off says a piece is taken away

parts.note: Lancelot is a knight of King Arthur's Round Table
a lot is an item to be sold at auction

explanation.surface: A knight's weapon to be auctioned off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weapon of knight' reads as one phrase; 'of' is only a link, and the knight is Lancelot.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance is a long spear carried by a mounted knight.

clue.text: Feature of writer with a sinister disposition

definitions.text: Feature of writer with a sinister disposition

parts.words: Feature of writer with a sinister disposition
parts.note: sinister suggests evil, but in Latin and heraldry it means left, so the writer favours the left hand

explanation.walkthrough: Sinister is Latin for left; in heraldry it means the bearer's left side.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing with the left hand is the trait of a person whose natural bent is to the left side.
